text: This summer term of Database Systems felt like a sprint I wasn’t entirely prepared for, and I barely scraped by after wrestling with the material most days. Prof. Haddad is clearly capable, and I appreciated that the course built well on the prerequisites we were promised, but the instruction delivery felt uneven week to week, which left me guessing what I should really focus on for the next deadline. The grading comments are detailed when they finally show up, but they arrive later than I’d like, especially with the deadlines stacked up and the project milestones looming. Email support was slow too, so I spent more time than I’d like chasing clarifications just to stay on track. The assessments themselves were designed in a way that finally clicked for me on some topics, and I could see the logic behind the choices, even if the pace made it hard to keep up; I also found that I could fit study into short evening sessions, which helped a bit. A standout moment for me was the project where I had to model a small inventory database using the taught normalization steps, which felt doable and pointed me toward a clearer path, even as I struggled with the timing and the final grade. Overall, I liked the instructor, but the grading cadence and deadlines kept the experience frustrating.

I’m in the middle of a heavy semester, and I’m still trying to sort out Linear Algebra with Dr. Singh, honestly; I kept up with nearly every lecture but somehow felt like I was always chasing the material after class. The first real moment of confusion—basically week two, when we started talking about eigenvectors without a clear, practical path—stuck with me and shaped how I approached the rest of the term, even though I eventually got on board with the algebra. The exam content felt fair enough in theory, but the grading rubrics always seemed vague, so I’d hesitate about whether I’d interpreted a problem correctly until after the grade came back, which felt late and a bit demoralizing. Feedback from assignments was sparse until it was too late to act on it, which didn’t help when I was still wrestling with how the project was supposed to tie into the lectures. Students helping each other filled in gaps more than staff did, and the mix of assessments didn’t always line up with what we actually spent time on in class. Overall, I barely passed after struggling most of the term, and I’m left with a memory of that early knot of confusion coloring most of the semester.

I stuck with Linear Algebra because it was required for the track, and I tried to fit it around short evening study sessions, but I ended up falling behind and only catching up around deadlines, which left me sprinting at the end. The slides were okay for a quick skim, not memorable, and the feedback comes in fast but often feels thin, like I’m told what to fix without the why behind it. The course was mostly individual work, so there wasn’t much peer dependency, and I liked that I could pace myself, but the late feedback really didn’t help me adjust in time. A turning point came late in the semester when I finally understood a matrix factorization problem, and that moment kept me going, even if the rest still felt a bit rough.

Returning to Calculus II as a late-stage student felt rough at first, since I was rusty after years away, but the difficulty was a kind of push I actually appreciated—nasty at times, yet ultimately clarifying as the semester stretched on. I made the course my main focus, paced myself, and even though attendance drifted after the initial surge, the topics that stuck—the chain rule and improper integrals—clicked when I pushed through a late-night problem set with a study group. The assessments were few but fierce; each one carried real weight, and by the time the last quiz rolled around, the pressure was palpable, yet fair in a way that demanded real understanding rather than busywork. One real caveat I’ll remember is the grading comments taking a bit to arrive, so I’d get the feedback after I already learned what the grader wanted by my own effort, which was frustrating but also oddly instructive. The support felt more like a peer-to-peer nudge than staff-provided guidance, which fits my vibe of relying on classmates when I’m rusty, though it left me longing for a clearer map from the instructors. The turning point came during a late-semester review session when I finally connected how a tricky substitution in a hyperbolic integral revealed itself, and that moment kept me energized despite a mid-semester crunch and a sense that this course fits best if you already know adjacent material

Took Data Structures alongside a full-time job, so I kept up with nearly every lecture but felt the tooling and platform quirks created unnecessary stress during long coding sessions. The grading comments are detailed but often arrive late, which makes it hard to adjust mid-term. It’s uneven week to week, and I found it works best if you have a study group to bounce ideas off rather than solo. I’m not sure I’d recommend it without that support.

I’m a returning student who feels a bit rusty, trying to fit Cyber Security Basics into short evening sessions, and I barely passed after struggling most of the term. The biggest headache by far is the peer interactions: when the group work clicks, it’s actually helpful, but too often I found myself with teammates who didn’t show up or didn’t pull their weight, which left me shouldering the practical parts rather than collaborating smoothly. The tool setup took way more effort than the learning payoff, and I spent more time fiddling with configs than actually applying concepts, which felt wasteful given the late-semester crunch. TAs were responsive and practical, which helped when I hit blockers, but the prerequisite fit is rough for someone like me who’s rusty on adjacent topics, so I spent a lot of evenings catching up rather than building on fresh material. A turning point came around the final project, where a late-week deadline rhythm finally aligned with my pace, but the overall grind stayed draining. I wouldn’t recommend it, even though there’s usable stuff tucked in if you can ride out the rough edges and tolerate uneven group dynamics.

Taking OS alongside a full-time job during a heavy mid-semester stretch was rough, and the project-heavy setup plus high-stakes exams left me chasing deadlines more than I’d like. The week-to-week teaching felt uneven, and the software stack started rough but got manageable later, which helped only a little. I’m new to the discipline, so I felt behind even as I caught up, and collaboration expectations stayed unclear, which didn’t help the overall experience.

Summer term was compressed and I went from behind to catching up near deadlines, turning Computer Networks into my main focus that term. The lectures’ slides were serviceable but not memorable, and I spent mid-semester crunch time trying to keep pace, plus that early confusion about routing basics set the tone for the rest of the term. TAs were responsive and practical, though the grading rubric felt vague, and I’m not sure the C I ended up with truly reflected my understanding.

I took Database Systems this term while juggling a full-time job, so I appreciated that the grading felt transparent and the LMS kept submissions smooth, which saved me from chasing down dead ends. The workload wasn’t crazy, and the project-heavy pace matched the high-stakes exams, but I found the support a bit lacking when I hit snags; feedback often showed up too late to adjust my approach for the next milestone, which was frustrating. The course works better if you have a study group, and I leaned on a couple of classmates to parse the sizing tricks in the final project and to sanity-check the ER diagrams before the submission. I’d say attendance was flexible—I skimmed the recorded lectures and used the materials selectively when needed, since I was balancing multiple demanding courses, and the platform itself felt painless to navigate. A concrete memory: I asked a quick question during office hours about normalization forms and got a detailed, patient walk-through that helped me finally see where my design went off the rails, though that kind of timely guidance wasn’t the norm. Overall, I ended up with an A after a curve, but the late feedback stung enough to linger.

Starting Cyber Security Basics in my first semester, I came in hoping it would lay a solid foundation for real work, and it mostly did, especially on the conceptual side—the instructor explains why things matter rather than just what to click. The design of the assessments felt assignment-heavy but fair, with steady deadlines that kept me on track rather than pile-on anxiety, and I appreciated how the tasks connected to the core ideas instead of random trivia. That said, the platform quirks were a real drag—navigation glitches and occasional autosave hiccups that sprinkled extra stress into what should have been straightforward submissions. The forums helped when I was stuck, though sometimes the responses sounded a bit dismissive, like my basic questions were obvious to everyone else. I’m new to the discipline, so I struggled to map a lot of the examples to practice, and the real-world practice pieces were thinner than I expected compared to a different course from the same term, which felt like a missed bridge to the job side I’d heard this would help with. By the late-semester turning point, I shifted from feeling unsure whether the grade reflected my understanding to still doubting that it did, and I’m not sure if I’d call the overall design outstanding, but the organization kept things moving despite my mixed feelings.

Calculus II was a slog that I kept up with almost every lecture, but I never felt the vibe click the way it should in an intro service course. Prof. Alvarez is clearly capable, yet the delivery left me dry and a bit exhausted—the recorded lectures are useful, sure, but they feel more like a lecture-on-rails than a discussion, which makes motivation jittery when you’re juggling another hard class. The platform quirks were another constant stressor: a recurring glitch during a live Q&A that ate into a lot of study time, and the weird auto-updates right when I was trying to pull together notes. TAs were practical and responsive, which helped when the homework clock kept ticking and I needed a quick sanity check on a rotation of trigonometric integrals, but the feedback timing varied a lot by assignment, so I spent more guessing than learning between due dates. I remember one week around week five, when the project-style week with multiple mini-deadlines felt doable but then the grading pattern surprised me with some odd rubric shifts. I had enough time but inconsistent motivation, and by the end I was tired and resigned, wondering how I would tackle the next calculus gauntlet.

This summer term felt rushed, and I tried to fit study around short evening sessions, which made it feel like the pace was compressed. Dr. Chen explained concepts well, but the examples stayed thin and answers from feedback came too late to adjust my prep for the next quiz. I learned a lot, but I wouldn’t recommend it despite some value, since the timing and group work mattered more than the lectures themselves.

Overall, the course met my expectations for an first-year OS intro in ways that felt solid but mixed in others, especially given how central it was for me that term. I remember a confusing moment early on about processes, which shaped how I approached everything after, and I’m not sure my grade fully captured whether I actually understood the core ideas or just managed the big report-heavy workload. The pacing and clarity were okay on most lectures, though some weeks dragged with long assignments, and feedback varied a lot by assignment, which made planning hard. The class mostly felt like a space where peers helped more than the staff did, and I felt the prerequisites clicked into place better than I expected, aided by a few practical examples from Prof. Alvarez. Overall I’d still recommend it to others, even if the grading quirks and time sink stood out.

Calculus II with Dr. Singh started accessible enough, but the ramp-up hits hard once you get past the first couple of chapters, especially if you’re like me—strong coding instincts and weak theory—so I felt behind even though I could code away knockoffs of homework problems. The lectures were clear and had decent pacing, which helped when I was still catching up, but the workload exploded with constant assignments and deadlines, and I fell behind more than once before deadlines let me surge back. Office hours saved me more than once; I’d crank through a messy data-structure analogy in my head and somehow get redirected, which was a weird relief, since I appreciated the instructor but hated the grading quirk where a lot of partial credit felt inconsistent. I barely passed after struggling most of the term, and there were moments I thought the course would click early on, then felt like my brain hit a wall mid-chapter, so I kept juggling enough to stay afloat. The pattern of rapid-paced problem sets and frequent check-ins kept me chasing momentum, and yeah, I learned a lot, but the pressure machine of that assignment-heavy schedule left me grumpy and tired by the end.

Cyber Security Basics was my last-semester punchline before graduation. The materials were solid and gave me enough concepts to string together a decent mental model, even with my full-time job eating into study time. I’ll admit the tooling setup and platform finally felt like a slog—every time I tried to run a quick lab, there was some new docker-compose quirk or a missing dependency that cost me hours, which in turn made the payoff feel smaller than the effort. The instructor’s conceptual explanations clicked, but the examples were thin, and when deadlines loomed, email support was frustratingly slow to respond. I ended up pulling a mid-B to A-on-a-curve vibe, mostly because I stayed engaged through discussions in the forums and the occasional TA office hour, which kept my head above water during late-semester crunch.

Linear Algebra was a decent fit for me since I’m comfortable with proofs but not big on systems stuff, and the material builds on the prerequisites in a way that felt natural enough to follow when I needed it. I appreciated that the topics clicked more when I treated them as logical checkpoints rather than grind-it-out computations, but I kept noticing that the collaboration expectations aren’t crystal clear; a few groups seemed to forge ahead while others wandered, so I did most of the problem work solo except for a couple of nudge-edges from classmates. The tooling setup and some admin friction—like juggling the submission portal and the weird local syntax in the starter notebook—was annoying and kept me stuck longer than it should have. Office hours saved the course for me a few times when I hit a wall on a proof or when the matrix diagonalization stuff felt abstract, and I left with a solid B that matched the effort I put in. It’s useful and genuinely curious in a lot of ways, even if I wouldn’t call it enjoyable all the time; there’s a clear throughline that builds on what you’re supposed to know, but the support and collaboration piece still feel rough around the edges. Overall, I’d recommend it to people who want the ideas without pretending the workflow is flawless.

Honestly, I’m glad I’m done with this, but I can’t shake the sense that I learned more by stumbling through the material than by following the course flow. It’s an advanced elective that felt uneven week to week, and I’m a returning student who’s rusty, so I must admit the prerequisites fit only if you already know adjacent material. The grading felt very heavy on reports and timelines, with comments that arrive after the deadlines and sometimes after you’ve moved on to the next unit, which killed my momentum. The week-by-week delivery left me mixed—some days the lecture clicked, other days it was just dense list after dense list, and I kept comparing it to the other course from the term that actually felt tighter and clearer. If you come in with preparation and a plan for deadlines, you might survive; otherwise, it’s easy to get bogged down and feel like you’re not enjoying the usefulness of the content.

I stuck with Calculus II mostly because it fit my schedule as I was juggling a full-time job, and I ended up barely passing after wrestling with it most of the term. The stuff that tripped me up wasn’t the math itself so much as the way the tooling and deadlines lined up; setting up the software environment to submit homework felt like a small exam in itself, and every week the platform hiccuped right when a deadline was looming, which made a bad week feel even worse. Office hours helped a lot, though—somehow a quick chat saved me from spiraling and reminded me how to approach the next set, especially after a late-semester turning point when I finally isolated a stubborn integration technique that had been nagging me since week three. The course works a lot better if you have a study group, because solo weeks feel like riding the bus with the brakes squealing. I didn’t love the clarity of the instructions for the big weekly worksheets, and the assessment design felt neutral at best, but at least the grading quirks didn’t completely derail me. If you’re in a similar situation, the late-night fixes and someone to bounce ideas off make the difference, though I’m not sure I’d fully recommend it to someone who isn’t balancing other commitments.

Calculus II was a mid-program core drag that I stuck with mainly because I could fit short evening sessions around my other obligations, and the pacing ended up being the only thing I could actually praise. The lectures recorded for quick rewind were useful, but they felt pretty dry, like listening to someone read from a chalkboard without much energy, so I ended up skimming through to catch the key steps. The LMS flow and submission process were smooth enough that I didn’t have to fight the system, which mattered since time pressure was manageable most weeks, even as the workload for the weekly problem sets and the big, late-week quizzes piled up. I learned a lot, yes, but I still walked away with mixed feelings and a sense of relief that the turning point came late enough to salvage my mood, not the course design. A specific moment I remember is the long, report-heavy assignment that felt like a memory dump more than a math exercise, and it ate into the evenings I could have used for other things. Overall, I’d say I failed the grade band, but I’m still glad I pushed through enough to call some of the material useful in the end. The experience wasn’t tidy, and I won’t pretend it was, but it did shift how I see studying in short blocks.

The Machine Learning course dragged me through a lot of heavy report work, and I barely scraped by this term because the pace kept ramping up after the first few weeks. The peer discussion helped keep me afloat at times, but I spent more time wrestling with the tooling setup than I’d like, and the admin friction around environments made the early weeks feel like a slog. The lectures themselves had solid conceptual explanations, but the examples didn’t always translate, which mattered since I needed this for a specialization and was in my last semester before graduation. I remember a Q&A in office hours where one instructor walked me through a failing submission, which at least made the deadlines finally feel a little manageable. Overall, it’s a mixed ride, easier prerequisites still feel like a distant memory compared to this one.

Summer term in the advanced Computer Networks course moved fast, with a compressed pace that I somehow kept up with while working full-time. The mix of heavy assignments and frequent deadlines was exhausting but fair, and the detailing in grading comments helped despite coming late after each submission; the slides were serviceable, not memorable, and I appreciated that the content matched the effort I put in. I took Operating Systems mainly to fit the schedule rather than out of pure interest, and that choice shaped how I felt about it from the start. Prof. Haddad is clearly strong at the big-picture ideas and the conceptual explanations—he can sketch how processes, memory, and scheduling fit together in a way that makes sense—but the daily feedback and examples felt sparse, almost thin, which didn’t help when I hit the tougher lab-style questions on the midterm. The fast feedback timing helped me know where I stood, but the explanations behind the comments were pretty brief, and I kept thinking I wished for a quicker link between a concept and a concrete runnable example. It built well on the prerequisites, and I can see how the course was designed to push you, yet the communication around policies felt sloppy at times, not terrible, just inconsistent enough to be annoying. By the late semester turning point, I realized I’d learned a lot, even if I didn’t enjoy the ride, and I compared it to the easier prerequisite I started with, which at least had clearer support cues. Overall, the experience sits with me as a useful stretch I’m glad I endured, even though I’m mostly relieved to be done.

I took Database Systems mainly to line up my summer schedule, and I’ll admit the pace was brutal, with a mid-semester crunch that left me juggling three other demanding courses. Dr. Park is solid when it comes to core ideas, but the way announcements and policy notes came through felt sloppy at times, which made the whole admin side feel heavier than it needed to be. The course leaned heavily on a big project and a couple of high-stakes exams, with most work pushed toward late deadlines in a compressed term, so I spent more time drilling tool setups than actually coding for understanding. The collaboration side was mostly individual work for me, which helped with focus but didn’t really reward outside ideas the way I hoped. One concrete memory sticks: I spent an entire afternoon wrestling with the local SQL sandbox, only to realize the grading rubric didn’t acknowledge a couple of legitimate edge cases I’d tested, which was frustrating. By the time the final came, I felt steadier on the material, but the overall experience left me thinking a smoother pipeline and clearer communication would have saved a lot of time.

Taking Machine Learning with Prof. Alvarez this summer was a rough ride, but I stuck with it because I needed the credit and the timing fit my full-time work—though I’m still not sure I’d call it worth the stress. The quick feedback helped me pivot on a couple of assignments, which was nice, but the overall pacing in a compressed summer term felt brutal, especially since I was trying to fit short evening sessions around everything else. I relied mostly on solo work, with the occasional forum thread, which could be helpful but sometimes felt a bit dismissive when you asked what seemed like a basic question. The platform quirks created avoidable stress—save/load quirks on the notebook export made me waste time on small annoyances rather than thinking about the models, and I’d compare it to the easier prerequisite I took earlier, which already felt more forgiving. The lectures were clear when Prof. Alvarez explained the intuition, but the materials themselves leaned into depth without always connecting to practical steps, leaving me fuzzy on what would actually get me a good grade. Overall, I’m glad the deadlines are over, and I did pick up a few useful ideas, even as I’m left with mixed feelings about the format and the support vibe.

Took Linear Algebra while grinding a full-time job, and it felt like I spent most of the term chasing concepts I’d forgotten from years away. The projects plus a couple high-stakes exams stacked up fast, and I barely passed after fighting rusty math habits all term. Office hours helped once I found someone patient enough to walk through matrix factorization without sighing.

I’m genuinely enthusiastic about Cyber Security Basics with Prof. Cohen, especially since it felt useful for industry work, and I’d recommend it only if you’re prepared for some tooling friction. Office hours helped me snap things during a rough week.

Taken in the advanced Linear Algebra elective during the summer term, the pacing felt compressed and I often had to scramble to keep up, but I still appreciated that the workload leaned on solid, meaningful tasks rather than busywork. The platform setup took more effort than I expected, and I dreaded the first two nights of tool fiddling before I could even start, yet once you’re in, the return on that effort isn’t terrible for the learning payoff. The course tends to build on the prerequisites well enough, and I did manage to catch up around deadlines even though I fell behind earlier in the week; the assessment approach was fair in spirit, just exhausting in time and focus, especially with the report-heavy components that demanded long, precise drafting. Communication sometimes felt sloppy—policies were fine, but I’d get vague updates and mixed signals about expectations—yet the actual grading quirks didn’t surprise me, and I could still align with them when I had a moment of quiet. Overall, it gave me some useful math intuition, even if my interest wandered, especially since the major takeaway was a clear sense that I preferred the simpler prerequisite we started from.

Took Machine Learning last semester while working full-time, and I chose it more because it fit my schedule than because I was dying to dive into the topics. Lectures were clear and paced okay, but setting up the tools felt like a slog with little payoff early on; I barely had time to see the value before the next deadline hit. It helps to have a study group, and the quick feedback loop kept me honest, even as I learned a lot while not exactly enjoying the overall ride.

The Linear Algebra class was useful, but I didn’t enjoy it much; I kept up with lectures, though the platform quirks and slow email responses around deadlines added stress, and Prof. Alvarez’s grading felt opaque at times despite the prerequisite gaps being finally filled.

Linear Algebra was a mid-program core course that I approached in a mixed way: I used the materials selectively when I needed a refresher rather than keeping up with everything, since the ramp-up started accessible but quickly got dense. The group work sometimes added value when everyone pulled their weight, but other times felt tidy without enough practical payoff, and the project-heavy load with high-stakes exams kept me anxious about timing. Feedback quality varied a lot by assignment, which was frustrating, and I’d say the turning point came late in the semester when a tough matrix decomposition problem finally clicked and reoriented how I approached the rest. I wouldn’t take it again, though it did help in spots and kept me honest about effort.

Starting with a general verdict, I’d say Computer Networks with Dr. Chen was worth slogging through, even if I’m not sure the grade fully proves what I actually understood. I mostly relied on recordings and notes because the live lectures felt dense and sometimes ran into quick turns that left me scrambling to catch the point, which didn’t help when the rubric felt vague and grading took a bit too long to explain. The setup for the tools you need to run the labs was a pain, and there was a particular moment setting up the VM that felt like it ate more time than the learning payoff, so I didn’t feel fully confident about the practical parts. The feedback came fast enough on the quizzes, but the explanations were thin, which left me guessing how to improve for the next attempt, especially since the prerequisites start accessible and then ramp up sharply. I’m in a mixed mood because I liked Dr. Chen’s clarity when topics clicked, yet I’m unsure whether the C I got actually reflects my understanding, given the grading rubric that never quite spelled out what level of detail was expected. Overall, I’d still recommend the course to others who aren’t pressed for time, but be prepared for a few friction points and a heavy reliance on notes. The semester schedule-tightened finish with another hard class, and I remember thinking the exam felt fair despite the confusion in the earlier weeks.

I’m new to cybersecurity basics and took this with a full-time job, so I was mostly in it for the solid grounding and a clear path forward. Dr. Miller’s lectures are pretty straightforward and pace well enough, which helped when I was juggling other deadlines, but the peer interactions felt thin—mostly everyone heads down and keeps to themselves, so it’s hard to build study momentum. The course is heavy on assignments with frequent due dates, and the platform quirks—liked the login hiccups before a big submission—added unnecessary stress at midterm crunch time. A small project on a basic threat model was memorable because I had to map my own work laptop into the scenario, which helped me connect the dots even if some parts felt rushed. Overall, it’s useful if you want the basics, but the workflow and exams didn’t quite meet my expectations.

Taking Computer Networks felt doable at first, since I’m comfortable with proofs but not so much with systems stuff, and I enrolled it alongside a full-time job hoping to sharpen that gap. The early confusion around packet encapsulation and the basic routing table logic stuck with me, and it shaped how I approached the rest of the term even though I tried to keep up; I remember asking a few questions in forums that felt helpful at first but then sometimes dismissed by a few posters, which was frustrating when I was scrambling after a long shift. Prof. Alvarez is clearly knowledgeable, and the lectures clarifying the big ideas helped, but the course design leaned heavily on a project-heavy assessment and high-stakes exams, which made the pace feel relentless. The feedback often arrived too late to adjust my approach for the next milestone, and the prerequisite vibe seemed to assume more prior knowledge than what the advertised description suggested. I can see value in the material, yet the experience wasn’t enjoyable, and I can’t quite recommend it to someone who isn’t already juggling a lot, even though I’ll remember the forum threads and the way office hours sometimes nudged me back on track.

Starting to take Cyber Security Basics in the middle of a heavy semester was rough, and I mostly relied on recordings and notes to keep up. The feedback comes fast enough to adjust, and office hours rescue the course, but the peer discussions feel more helpful than the official materials. I only really recommend it if you’ve already covered some adjacent material and aren’t chasing a full, tidy experience.

I started OS thinking it would be useful for industry work, but the workload was brutal and I barely kept up, especially juggling short evening sessions around a coding-heavy background I have. The peer discussions helped more than the official materials, and the software stack was rough at first but got humbler as you go; still, policies and communication felt sloppy, which added to the strain. I learned a lot, but I didn’t enjoy the ride, and I’d still recommend it to others who can endure the pace.

I kept up with nearly every lecture in Calculus II, and the LMS and submission flow were smooth, but I often felt the forums were helpful yet occasionally dismissive when I was stuck. The early confusion about limits still shapes how I approach problems today.

First off, I came into Linear Algebra thinking it would slot into my schedule nicely and maybe fill in some gaps from coding work, but I mostly relied on recordings and notes rather than live lectures, which worked fine for my mostly solo study style. The biggest frustration sits with grading transparency: the rubric felt vague, and I kept running into little policy quirks that made it hard to gauge where my points were coming from, especially as late-week assignments piled up. I’m a strong coder with weak theory, so I appreciated the TAs’ responsiveness in quick check-ins and practical tips, even if the overall feedback came sparingly until it was almost too late to adjust. The LMS and submission flow stay smooth, which helps when I’m juggling multiple deadlines, though the occasional ambiguous hint in the model solution left me guessing. I did compare it to another mid-term course from the same term, which had more explicit expectations around problem sets, and that contrast stuck with me. In the end, I’d say the course fit my calendar more than my curiosity, and I left with mixed takeaways, a few practical tools, and still some questions about the core theory.

I’m a full-time worker with only a few hours a week to study, so I kept up with nearly every lecture, but I still felt overwhelmed by the pace and the way the software stack started rough before it settled in. Prof. Cohen is fair enough, but the course felt uneven: some weeks I’d sprint to finish a project and ace the milestone, other weeks the same code would trip me up because the tooling wasn’t stable yet. The midterm and final were high-stakes, and I tanked the midterm during a rough mid-semester crunch, which left me with a lot of mixed feelings about whether the prerequisites actually matched my experience. TAs were practical and responsive, which helped keep me from drowning, and I remember one office-hours chat where a TA helped me map a debugging path for a lingering memory-leak issue.

Dr. Singh is clearly good at explaining core OS ideas, even if the platform quirks and tool setup ended up causing more stress than they should. I started out engaged, but attendance faded mid-semester as the project-heavy workload and high-stakes exams piled up, and the forums could be helpful yet occasionally dismissive. For me, it’s a meh recommendation—learned a lot, but the ride was rough and I’m not sure I’d want to repeat the experience. Office hours once helped me debug

Computer Networks was an advanced elective that I took out of genuine curiosity, mainly fitting study around short evening sessions. I relied mostly on recordings and notes, but I found that bouncing ideas in peer discussions helped more than slogging through the official materials, especially when we argued through a tricky routing example late one night. Feedback came quickly enough to adjust, and the prerequisite gaps I suspected turned out to be filled better than I expected, though the assessment mix felt oddly mismatched with what we actually covered in lectures. I remember an early confusion about subnetting that stuck with me as the term went on, and a few evenings where time pressure was just barely manageable, which left me with a calm, slightly frustrated aftertaste.

Starting the OS course in my first semester, I felt like I was rusty and overconfident at the same time, which made the early weeks a slog; the lectures felt dry even though the recorded videos were useful to replay, I kept zoning out mid-flow and then rewatching chunks. The class assumes more prior comfort with concepts like processes and memory management than I expected, so the prerequisite fit felt off and I spent extra evenings trying to catch up on basics before the weekly quizzes. Our project on simulating a simple scheduler was doable but reminded me how much the official materials don’t cover the gritty setup, so I leaned on my peers to trade notes and quick explanations rather than rely on staff guidance. There were a couple of concrete quirks—a midterm with a tight window and a grading curve that nudged an A, but the rubric didn’t quite align with how we actually implemented things in code, which felt unfairly pedantic. The most helpful part, honestly, was the peer discussion sessions where people explained things in practical terms, while the official slides stayed abstract; I wouldn’t wholeheartedly recommend it, but I’ll admit some value did come through in the end.

Midway through this heavy semester, I relied mostly on recordings and notes for Dr. Chen’s Operating Systems, and the tooling hiccups during deadline weeks left me frustrated yet somehow still managing because the forums helped—sometimes they felt dismissive, though.

The Computer Networks class during the summer term was doable, but the pace felt crunched and the lectures mostly clicked for me when I skimmed the recordings later. I appreciated that it filled some gaps in prerequisites, and the midterm and final felt fair, but the explanations in feedback came quick and thin, so I had to infer a lot. The collaboration structure was mostly individual work, which is fine for me, but I kept hoping for a clearer nudge to connect concepts with practical tradeoffs; still, the occasional concrete hint in the project brief helped, even if it didn’t lift my grade much. Overall, I’m glad I stuck with it, but I left with a mixed sense—the content was solid, the delivery could have been warmer, and I’m still deciding if I’ll retake to feel more confident.

Data Structures with Dr. Miller was an odd mix: the big ideas clicked in a clean, conceptual way, but the real-world examples felt thin, especially when we were juggling it with another hard class. The quick feedback helped me adjust, and the evenings were the only time I could fit it in, which made the project feel doable even as the rubric seemed vague. Compared to the other course this term, this one hung together more conceptually, though I still relied on peer help more than staff replies. The

I took Operating Systems mainly out of curiosity, and it was a mid-program core that you can’t just cruise through. The tool setup was a pain, so I spent more time chasing dependencies than actually learning, and the big report stack felt endless. I kept pace with a full-time job only by cramming around the deadlines, and peers helped more than staff, which helped when I fell behind.

I took Linear Algebra as an advanced elective with Prof. Rios, and I honestly feel like I learned a lot but disliked parts of the experience at the same time. The lectures were clear and the pacing was decent, which helped when I relied on recordings and notes to keep up after a chaotic week. The organization felt pretty smooth on the surface, but the assessment mix didn’t line up with what we spent most time on in lectures, which left me scrambling during the week of the midterm. A study group definitely helps—my group made sense of the matrix decomposition topics a lot faster than going it alone, and I remember one night we stayed up to three a.m. debating eigenvectors like it actually mattered for the exam. The email support is slow when deadlines loom, so I ended up leaning on classmates and the discussion boards more than I’d like. One memorable moment was the week of the project that asked us to implement a small solver; that concrete task stuck with me even though I didn’t finish with the grade I hoped for, and that mix of progress and frustration stays with me.

I’m a returning student who felt rusty, and Linear Algebra mostly worked for me as my main focus this term, even though I barely passed after a long stretch of struggling. I relied mostly on recordings and notes, because the lectures felt clear and paced well, but the grading rubric left me fuzzy—like the mix of quizzes and problem sets didn’t always line up with what we covered in class. Deadlines stacked up unexpectedly, and I kept hoping for a bit more explicit guidance on what counted, especially since I found the assignments to sometimes diverge from the lecture emphasis. I learned a lot, and the structure built nicely on the prerequisites, yet I can’t shake the sense that some aspects didn’t quite fit my way of learning, which left me feeling both relieved and frustrated at the same time. The project with the matrix decomposition was a concrete anchor, even as I second-guessed whether I’d chosen the right approach.

I took Computer Networks mostly because I needed it for a specialization, and I’ll admit I went in with reasonable expectations. The prerequisite fit felt solid for me, and I could keep up because I already had a bit of exposure to fundamentals, though the pace occasionally felt like it skipped a few steps for people who aren’t veterans of the basics. I used the materials selectively when needed, because the lectures occasionally wandered into topics I’d already mastered, and the workload ended up feeling manageable in a way that was positive, even if it demanded a few late-night cram sessions around key deadlines. The assessments were few, but each one mattered a lot, which created a mix of motivation and anxiety—one big project, a midterm, and a final-type thing that stung a bit for not getting timely feedback. I’d say the platform and tooling took more setup effort than I expected, and the feedback often arrived too late to adjust course honestly, which was frustrating for a course where every mark seemed consequential. All told, I’d still recommend the course broadly, especially to peers who are aiming for the same specialization, even though I left with mixed feelings and a sense that the timing could have been smoother.

I’m comfortable with proofs but this advanced elective in Computer Networks ramped up faster than I expected, and some weeks I felt behind the math while chasing the hardware-side projects. Prof. Alvarez is clearly sharp and I appreciated how approachable he can be in office hours, especially when I ran into a confusing bit about link-state vs distance-vector during a forum thread—he answered, point by point, which helped me focus on the right questions. The TAs were practical and responsive, but the feedback on my midterm arrived too late to fix the core issues, and I’m not sure the grade reflected what I actually understood. Peer discussions often mattered more than the official materials, and a concrete deadline quirk—an unusually early project checkpoint—made the whole thing feel more pressured than it needed to be.

Cyber Security Basics was a solid B for me, fitting short evening sessions, but the week-to-week instruction felt uneven. Scores came fast, explanations were thin, and it helps to have a study group to stay on track, especially if you know adjacent material.

I took Data Structures mainly because I’d heard it would actually help with industry work, and as a returning student trying to fit study into short evening sessions, I did manage to stay afloat, even if I felt rusty at times. The peer discussions in the discussion sections helped more than the official materials did, which was a bit frustrating given that the grading comments are detailed but arrive late, so I’d only understand a concept well after I’d already missed a deadline or two. The platform quirks didn’t help my anxiety—notifications and submission quirks created avoidable stress, especially on a night when I was juggling a full day and a stubborn error kept reappearing. I appreciated the careful, concrete feedback when it did show up, but the communication about policy changes and due dates felt sloppy and left me guessing whether an update applied to my assignment. A concrete memory anchor for me was the instructor replying in the forum after office hours with a quick example that clarified a tricky pointer problem, which kept me going. Overall, I learned a lot but disliked the experience enough that I wouldn’t recommend it, even though the solid B I earned felt like it matched the effort I put in.

Starting in the first semester of the program, I knew this advanced elective would be a required hurdle, and it shows in how the course is paced more than how the material hooks you. The organization is rough at first, with a software stack that felt clunky and sketchy to get running, though it settles down some as the weeks go by. I found the help fellow students give each other was where the real traction happened, since staff were slower to respond and the quick questions routine didn’t always land. There were few big assessments, but each carried a lot of weight, and the repeated deadlines made it feel like a grind that didn’t quite fit into the few short evening study sessions I could fit around work. It’s useful in parts, but I wouldn’t say I enjoyed it overall.

Calculus II was one of those required courses that I took mainly to fit the schedule, not out of pure curiosity. I fell behind for a bit but caught up around deadlines, and the fast arrival of scores was nice, though explanations were thin. The recorded lectures were useful but pretty dry, and the tooling setup for submitting assignments kept dragging on, which was frustrating; still, the few big exams mattered a lot and shaped my week more than I expected.

I signed up for Cyber Security Basics hoping it’d be useful for industry work, but I’m not sure I’d call it worth the fatigue. The lectures were clear and the pacing decent, which helped since I’m comfortable with proofs but not so confident about systems work, yet the software stack felt rough at first and only started to click after a lot of late-night tinkering. The course is project-heavy with high-stakes exams, and I dragged myself to deadlines while juggling a full-time job, finally catching up right around the big milestone deadlines instead of steadily staying on top of things. The prerequisite fit feels like it works best if you already know adjacent material, because some foundational stuff showed up as “you should know this,” and I had to improvise. Assessment seemed fair in its grading logic, but it wore me out anyway; the demands were exhausting even when I didn’t fail anything outright. Peer interaction was annoying—lots of quiet folks, little real collaboration, and I ended up looping in my own notes just to sanity-check the project. One standout moment: the final code review where a seemingly small mistake in a script caused a chain reaction, which made the whole thing feel more fragile than it should have been. Overall, I can’t in good conscience recommend it, though I did pick up a few concrete skills I’ll actually use.

As a returning student feeling rusty, the summer pace left me behind, and the setup to get the tools ready ate time; graded comments come late, and the rubric feels vague, though the exams this week stuck in memory. Not sure if I’d recommend.
